analogy.p: Imagine a crowd of people humming. As more energy is put in (a hotter object), the whole crowd gets louder (greater intensity), and the main note they hum rises to a higher pitch (shorter wavelength). A matt black surface is like an open mouth that lets sound out easily, and a shiny silver surface is like a hand clamped over the mouth that sends sound back in. The analogy breaks down because radiation is an electromagnetic wave, not sound, and an object emits a whole range of wavelengths at once rather than a single note.
analogy.t: A choir of voices getting louder and higher

bullets: Every object emits infrared radiation, even a block of ice, because its particles have thermal energy.
The **hotter** the object, the **more** infrared it emits in a given time.
A **perfect black body** absorbs all radiation incident on it, and neither reflects nor transmits any.
A **good absorber is also a good emitter**; a poor absorber is also a poor emitter.
The **intensity** and **wavelength distribution** of the emitted radiation depend on temperature.
The required practical (Required Practical 10) compares different surfaces, usually with a **Leslie cube** and an infrared detector.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA Physics (triple science only) asks you to know that all bodies, whatever their temperature, emit and absorb infrared radiation; that the hotter a body is, the more infrared radiation it radiates in a given time; that a perfect black body absorbs all the radiation that falls on it and does not reflect or transmit any; that a good absorber is also a good emitter; and that the intensity and the wavelength distribution of the radiation depend on the temperature of the body. You must also be able to carry out and evaluate the required practical that investigates how the amount of infrared radiation absorbed or radiated by a surface depends on the nature of that surface. The big idea is that **temperature and surface** control how much radiation an object gives out and takes in.

bullets: Infrared is an electromagnetic wave: it travels at the speed of light in a vacuum and **needs no medium**.
All bodies emit infrared, **whatever their temperature**; even cold objects do, just less.
All bodies also **absorb** infrared from their surroundings.
If a body **absorbs more than it emits**, its temperature rises; if it **emits more than it absorbs**, its temperature falls.
If absorption and emission are equal, the temperature stays **constant**.
Infrared is a form of **thermal radiation**, one of the ways of transferring energy thermally (along with conduction and convection).
core.p: **Infrared radiation** is part of the electromagnetic spectrum with wavelengths longer than visible red light. All objects emit it because the particles in any object above absolute zero have thermal (kinetic) energy, and this energy is transferred to the surroundings as electromagnetic waves. You can feel infrared as warmth when you hold your hand near a hot object without touching it; it needs no medium, so it can travel through a vacuum, which is how energy reaches us from the Sun. Because every body emits and absorbs infrared at the same time, an object at a steady temperature is simply one where the amount it absorbs equals the amount it emits.

bullets: At a **higher temperature** the particles have more energy, so more radiation is emitted **each second**.
The emitted radiation also covers a **different mix of wavelengths** as temperature changes.
A thermal imaging camera detects this infrared and displays hotter objects as brighter or warmer colours.
The **difference** between an object's temperature and its surroundings controls the **net** energy transfer.
An object cooling in a room loses energy quickly while it is much hotter, then more slowly as it nears room temperature.
Objects that are 'red hot' or 'white hot' are so hot that they emit visible light as well as infrared.
core.h: The hotter the object, the more it radiates
core.p: The rate at which an object emits infrared radiation increases as its temperature increases. A kettle of boiling water radiates much more infrared every second than a cup of lukewarm water of the same size and surface. This is why a hot object feels warmer when you hold your hand a few centimetres away, and why thermal imaging cameras can pick out warm bodies against a cooler background. It also explains why a hot object loses its energy to the surroundings quickly at first and more slowly as it cools: its rate of emission falls as its temperature falls.

bullets: A perfect black body **absorbs all** radiation incident on it, at every wavelength.
It **does not reflect** and **does not transmit** any radiation.
Absorbed radiation makes the body heat up, so a good absorber warms quickly.
A perfect black body is also the **best emitter**: at a given temperature it emits more radiation than any other body of the same surface area.
The Sun and the stars are often modelled as black bodies.
A real **matt black surface** is a good approximation to a black body, while a **shiny silver surface** is the opposite.
core.p: A **perfect black body** is an idealised object that **absorbs all of the radiation incident on it**. It does not reflect any radiation and does not transmit any radiation through it. Real objects are never perfect, but matt black surfaces come very close. Because absorbed radiation heats the body up, a perfect black body is also the **best possible emitter** at any given temperature. This might seem strange, since 'black' sounds like it should not send anything out, but a black body is only black at low temperatures when it emits no visible light; at high temperatures it glows brightly.

bullets: Matt black: **good absorber, good emitter**, poor reflector.
Shiny silver or white: **poor absorber, poor emitter**, good reflector.
The surface (not the colour inside) controls the rate of energy transfer by radiation.
A hot object with a matt black surface cools **faster** by radiation than the same object with a shiny surface.
A cold object with a matt black surface **warms faster** by absorbing radiation than a shiny one.
Applications: **foil blankets**, **vacuum flasks** with silvered walls, solar panels painted black, radiators with matt finish, houses painted white in hot countries.
core.p: The surface of an object affects how it absorbs and emits radiation. **Dark, matt surfaces** are good absorbers and good emitters; **light, shiny surfaces** are poor absorbers and poor emitters because they **reflect** most of the radiation that arrives. The link between absorption and emission is not a coincidence: the same properties of the surface control both. This is why a car left in the Sun with a black interior heats up quickly, and why a shiny silver blanket is used to keep a casualty warm, since it reflects the infrared from the body back instead of letting it escape.

bullets: **Intensity** means the power of radiation per unit area; on the graph it is the height of the curve.
The curve for a **hotter** body is **higher at all wavelengths** than the curve for a cooler body.
The **peak** of the curve shifts to a **shorter wavelength** (to the left) as temperature increases.
The area under the curve represents the **total radiation emitted**, which rises sharply with temperature.
A relatively cool object such as a person emits mostly infrared; a very hot object such as a star also emits visible and ultraviolet.
Hotter stars look **blue-white**; cooler stars look **red**, because their peak wavelengths differ.
core.h: How temperature affects intensity and wavelength
core.p: The infrared (and other radiation) emitted by an object is not at one single wavelength but spread across a range. The graph of **intensity** against **wavelength** for a body at a given temperature has a single peak. As the temperature of the body increases, two things happen: the **intensity of every wavelength increases**, so the whole curve gets higher, and the **peak wavelength moves to a shorter wavelength**. This is why a heated piece of metal first glows dull red, then orange, then yellow-white as its temperature rises: the peak moves toward the visible region and more of the shorter visible wavelengths are emitted.

bullets: Read the **peak wavelength** from the horizontal axis directly below the highest point of each curve.
The curve with the **highest peak** and the **shortest peak wavelength** belongs to the **hottest** body.
Describe the **trend**: 'as the temperature increases, the peak moves to shorter wavelength and its height increases'.
Do not say the curves 'move up and down' only; mention **wavelength** for the shift and **intensity** for the height.
Curves for different temperatures **do not cross** on a standard black body diagram (hotter is above colder at every wavelength).
If asked about total energy emitted, link it to the **area under the curve**.
core.p: Exam questions often give a graph with two or three curves for different temperatures and ask you to describe or compare them. Treat the axes carefully: wavelength is on the horizontal axis (increasing to the right) and intensity is on the vertical axis. To compare two curves, state which curve is higher, state where each peak lies, and say what this means for temperature. When asked to 'identify the hottest object', pick the curve that is highest and whose peak is furthest to the left. Always refer to the data by quoting wavelengths read off the axis where numbers are given.

bullets: **Independent variable**: the surface of the face (matt black, shiny black, matt white, shiny silver).
**Dependent variable**: the infrared radiation emitted, measured as a reading on the detector (or as a temperature rise).
**Control variables**: temperature of the water/cube, distance from the face to the detector, size of the face, angle and position of the detector, time of measurement, and the same detector.
The Leslie cube has four different faces so the water temperature is the same for all, giving a **fair test**.
An alternative uses **identical metal plates** with different surfaces placed the same distance from a heater, measuring temperature rise after a set time.
The aim is to show that **matt black surfaces emit (and absorb) the most** and **shiny silver surfaces the least**.
core.p: The required practical investigates how the **nature of a surface** affects the amount of infrared radiation it **emits** (or absorbs). The independent variable is the type of surface (for example matt black, shiny black, matt white, shiny silver); the dependent variable is the amount of infrared radiation detected (a reading on an infrared detector, or temperature change in a thermometer). The usual apparatus is a **Leslie cube**: a metal cube, hollow, filled with hot water, whose four vertical faces have different surface finishes. Because all four faces are at the same temperature (the water heats them evenly), any difference in the radiation emitted is due to the **surface** alone.

bullets: 1. Place the Leslie cube on a **heat-proof mat** and fill it with **hot (just boiled) water**, noting the temperature with a thermometer.
2. Place the **infrared detector** (thermopile or detector with meter) a fixed distance (for example 10 cm) from the **first face**, with the detector facing the face.
3. Record the **detector reading** once it has settled, after a fixed time such as 30 seconds.
4. **Rotate the cube** (or move the detector) to the next face, keeping the **same distance** and angle, and record the reading again.
5. Repeat for all four faces, then **repeat the whole set** at least 2 more times and calculate a **mean** for each face.
6. Check that the water temperature is the same each time (top up with hot water if necessary).
7. Plot a **bar chart** (categoric variable) of mean reading against surface.
**Safety**: hot water can scald, so use a stable surface, pour carefully, and do not touch the hot faces; wear eye protection if advised.
core.h: Required practical: method step by step
core.p: A clear, ordered method is worth up to six marks in a written question, so know it well. The key points are to keep everything fixed except the surface, to wait for stable readings, and to repeat. Using a data logger or a digital meter gives more precise readings than a person reading a dial. Hot water is dangerous, so safety also matters.

bullets: **Conclusion**: matt black emits the most infrared radiation; shiny silver the least; the rate of emission depends on the surface, not just on temperature.
Because the cube cools, readings taken later may be lower; **take readings quickly** or keep water hot and replace it.
Possible **errors**: draughts, other heat sources in the room, detector not the same distance, detector not at 90 degrees to the face, differences in water temperature.
**Improvements**: use a **data logger**, a clamp stand to fix the detector distance, a **thermometer** in the cube, and screen the detector from other radiation sources.
Take **repeat readings** and calculate the mean to reduce the effect of random errors; spot and exclude any **anomalous** results.
Check the **zero reading** of the detector before starting (background radiation) and subtract it if necessary.
Because the faces may differ in thickness or contact with the water, the result is a **comparison**, not a precise measurement.
core.h: Required practical: results, conclusions and improvements
core.p: Typically the matt black face gives the highest reading and the shiny silver face the lowest, with matt white and shiny black in between. The conclusion is that **matt (dull) black surfaces are the best emitters** of infrared and **shiny silver surfaces are the worst**, which agrees with the idea that good absorbers are good emitters. A good evaluation names sources of error and suggests specific improvements rather than vague statements like 'be more careful'.

bullets: **Setup**: identical plates (same material, size and thickness) at the same starting temperature, same distance from the heater.
**Measure** the temperature rise after the same time (for example 5 minutes).
The **matt black** plate warms up **faster** because it is a good absorber.
The **shiny** plate warms more slowly because it **reflects** most of the radiation.
Control the **distance**, **starting temperature**, **heating time** and **power of the heater**.
This shows the link: a surface that **absorbs well** is also the surface that **emits well**.
core.h: Variation: absorption of infrared by different surfaces
core.p: The practical can also investigate **absorption** rather than emission. Two identical metal plates, one matt black and one shiny silver, are placed the same distance from a source of infrared such as a lamp or radiant heater. A thermometer or temperature sensor is attached to the back of each plate, and the temperature rise is measured after a fixed time. The plate with the greater temperature rise has absorbed more radiation. In this version the **independent variable** is again the surface and the **dependent variable** is the temperature rise, with control of distance, time and the starting temperature of the plates.

bullets: **Solar panels** (heating): matt black to absorb as much infrared and visible radiation as possible.
**Vacuum flask**: silvered inner surfaces reflect radiation back into the liquid; the vacuum stops conduction and convection.
**Foil blanket** for casualties: shiny side reflects the body's infrared back, reducing energy loss.
**Heat sinks** and car engines: matt black fins emit radiation efficiently.
**Houses in hot countries** are often painted white to reflect radiation and absorb less.
**Link to the Earth's temperature**: the balance between radiation absorbed and radiation emitted determines the Earth's temperature.
**Link to energy transfers**: thermal radiation is one way energy is dissipated, relevant to efficiency calculations.
**Link to EM spectrum**: infrared is detected using special detectors, and wavelengths shorter than infrared become more intense as temperature rises.
core.p: The ideas above explain many familiar devices. Radiators are often painted matt, and **cooling fins** on electrical equipment are matt black to emit radiation well. Solar thermal panels are painted matt black to **absorb** as much as possible. In contrast, **space blankets** and **vacuum flasks** use shiny silver surfaces to **reflect** radiation and reduce energy transfer. These applications are often exam questions where you must link the surface type to absorption or emission and explain the effect on temperature.

bullets: Absorbed radiation increases the **internal energy** of the object, which usually shows as a temperature rise.
Emitted radiation decreases the internal energy of the emitter.
**Absorb faster than emit**: temperature rises. **Emit faster than absorb**: temperature falls.
**Equal rates**: constant temperature (equilibrium).
A surface can reflect, absorb or transmit; the three fractions together make up all the incident radiation.
A perfect black body reflects and transmits none, so everything incident is absorbed.
Shiny surfaces mostly reflect, so they gain and lose energy by radiation slowly.
core.h: Absorption, reflection and emission: the energy balance
core.p: When infrared radiation reaches a surface, it can be absorbed, reflected or transmitted. The absorbed part increases the internal energy of the object, so its temperature rises. At the same time the object emits infrared of its own. If it absorbs radiation faster than it emits, it warms up; if it emits faster than it absorbs, it cools; if the two rates are equal, its temperature stays constant. This balance is the idea behind the Earth's temperature and behind why a car left in the sun gets hot.

bullets: Link the surface type to absorption or emission in the same sentence as the observation.
Name the quantity measured (infrared detected) rather than just 'heat'.
For graphs, quote the direction of change for both intensity and peak wavelength.
For methods, mention the control variables and repeating to find a mean.
Use data in conclusions: compare readings with units.
A safety mark is usually for hot water: a heat-proof mat and care when pouring.
Spell wavelength, intensity and infrared correctly; marks depend on precise words.
core.h: Command words and how to score the marks
core.p: Questions on this point follow predictable patterns. 'State' wants a short fact such as 'a black body absorbs all radiation incident on it'. 'Explain' wants a reason linked to a property, such as 'matt black is a good absorber so the plate gets hotter'. 'Describe' on a graph wants the trend at all wavelengths plus the movement of the peak. 'Evaluate' on the practical wants a named weakness with a matching improvement. Always use the words absorb, emit, reflect, intensity and wavelength in the way the specification does.

exam: **State and recall questions (1 to 2 marks)**: all bodies emit and absorb infrared radiation; the hotter the body the more it emits in a given time; a perfect black body absorbs all radiation and does not reflect or transmit any.
**Explain surface questions (2 to 3 marks)**: say matt black is a good absorber and a good emitter, shiny silver reflects most radiation so is a poor absorber and a poor emitter.
**Graph description (3 to 4 marks)**: as temperature increases, the peak moves to a shorter wavelength and the intensity increases at all wavelengths; quote values where the graph has numbers.
**Method question (up to 6 marks)**: hot water in Leslie cube, same distance, detector reading each face, repeat, mean; mention safety and control variables.
**Variables (3 marks)**: independent = surface; dependent = infrared detected; control = distance, water temperature, size of face.
**Evaluation (3 to 4 marks)**: give a specific source of error and a specific improvement, for example a data logger or fixed clamp.
**Conclusion (2 marks)**: link results to the idea that matt black emits the most and shiny silver the least, quoting readings.
**Bar chart (categoric data)**: use bars with gaps, label axes with units, and plot the mean values.
**Command word 'Suggest'**: apply the idea (absorbers/emitters) to an unfamiliar context such as a satellite or flask.
**Use the exact words**: 'absorbs all the radiation incident on it', 'does not reflect or transmit', 'intensity', 'wavelength distribution'.
**Link answers**: connect temperature, intensity and wavelength explicitly in 4 and 6 mark questions.
**Safety marks**: mention hot water and scalding, and say how to reduce the risk (stable surface, pour carefully, handle with care).

mistakes.r: All objects emit infrared radiation, whatever their temperature; hotter objects emit more.
mistakes.w: Says only hot objects emit infrared radiation.

mistakes.r: A black body is a good absorber and a good emitter; it is black only when it is cool enough not to emit visible light.
mistakes.w: Says black objects do not emit radiation because they are black.

mistakes.r: Shiny silver surfaces are poor emitters and poor absorbers because they reflect radiation.
mistakes.w: Says shiny surfaces are good emitters because they are bright.

mistakes.r: A perfect black body reflects none and transmits none; it absorbs all radiation incident on it.
mistakes.w: Says a black body reflects some radiation.

mistakes.r: Say the infrared radiation emitted from each face is detected by the detector at a fixed distance.
mistakes.w: Writes 'the heat comes off the cube' in the method.

mistakes.r: Control the distance, angle and position of the detector, and the water temperature, so only the surface changes.
mistakes.w: Forgets to keep the distance from the detector the same for each face.

mistakes.r: As temperature rises, the peak moves to a shorter wavelength and the intensity increases at all wavelengths.
mistakes.w: Describes the peak moving to longer wavelength when temperature rises.

mistakes.r: Intensity increases at every wavelength as the temperature increases.
mistakes.w: Says the intensity decreases as the temperature increases.

mistakes.r: Name the control variables: the water temperature, distance to the detector, size of the face and time.
mistakes.w: Writes 'make it a fair test' without stating what is controlled.

mistakes.r: Absorbing infrared increases the internal energy of an object; the temperature rise follows from that.
mistakes.w: Says the object 'soaks up heat' without mentioning energy or radiation.

summary: The specification asks you to know that all bodies emit and absorb infrared radiation, that hotter bodies emit more, that a perfect black body absorbs all incident radiation, that good absorbers are good emitters, and that intensity and wavelength distribution depend on temperature. You must also carry out and evaluate the required practical on how surface type affects infrared radiation, which links to energy transfer, the Earth's temperature and everyday devices.

svg.cap: Black body radiation: intensity against wavelength for the same object at three temperatures. Every curve has a single peak. As the temperature rises (1) the intensity increases at every wavelength, so the area under the curve (total energy radiated each second) gets bigger, and (2) the peak moves to a shorter wavelength. Peaks are placed using Wien's law (peak wavelength = 2898 µm K / T); heights are exaggerated for clarity. A cool object peaks in the infrared; a very hot one peaks in the visible.

Surface and radiation. Top: matt black surfaces absorb most of the infrared that hits them (little is reflected), so they warm up fastest. Shiny silver surfaces reflect most of it, so they are poor absorbers. Bottom: for the same temperature, a matt black surface emits much more infrared each second than a shiny silver one. A good absorber is a good emitter; a poor absorber is a poor emitter. A perfect black body is the extreme case: it absorbs all radiation that hits it and emits the maximum for its temperature.

svg.cap: Left to right the electromagnetic spectrum runs from long-wavelength radio waves to short-wavelength gamma rays; infrared sits just beyond red light. Every object, whatever its temperature, emits infrared radiation and absorbs it from its surroundings. The hotter the object, the more infrared it emits each second (more arrows), which is why a boiling kettle gives out far more than a cube of ice.

terms.d: Electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths longer than visible red light, emitted by all objects.
Energy transferred as infrared electromagnetic waves from a hot object.
An object that absorbs all of the radiation incident on it and does not reflect or transmit any.
An object that gives out radiation.
An object that takes in radiation, increasing its internal energy.
The power of radiation per unit area; on a black body graph, the height of the curve.
The range of wavelengths emitted by an object and how much of each is emitted.
The wavelength at which an object emits the most intense radiation; it decreases as temperature increases.
A hollow metal cube filled with hot water, with four faces of different surface finishes, used to compare infrared emission.
A dull, rough surface that scatters rather than reflects light; a good absorber and emitter when dark.
A smooth surface that reflects most radiation; a poor absorber and emitter.
The variable you deliberately change, here the surface of the face.
The variable you measure, here the infrared radiation detected.
A variable kept the same to make the test fair, such as distance and water temperature.
A measurement that does not fit the pattern and should be checked, repeated or excluded.
To bounce radiation off a surface instead of absorbing it.
To let radiation pass through a material without being absorbed; a perfect black body transmits none.
The total kinetic and potential energy of the particles in an object; absorbing radiation increases it.
The state where an object absorbs radiation at the same rate as it emits it, so its temperature is constant.

worked.ans: The independent variable is the surface and the dependent variable is the detector reading. The same distance, angle, time and water temperature are controlled. Each face is measured and repeated, and means are compared; matt black should give the highest reading and shiny silver the lowest. Safety: use a stable mat and pour hot water carefully.
worked.q: Describe how you would investigate whether the surface of an object affects the amount of infrared radiation it emits. (6 marks)
steps: Fill a Leslie cube with hot water and place it on a heat-proof mat, checking the temperature.
Place an infrared detector the same distance (for example 10 cm) from the first face, facing it.
Record the reading after a fixed time, then rotate the cube and record each face in turn.
Repeat the readings and calculate a mean for each surface.
Keep the water temperature, distance, detector position and time the same.
Use care with hot water to avoid scalds.

worked.ans: The matt black plate absorbs more of the infrared radiation, while the shiny silver plate reflects most of it, so the black plate gains more energy and has a larger temperature rise.
worked.q: A student sees that a matt black plate is hotter than a shiny silver plate after both are placed the same distance from a heater for 5 minutes. Explain why. (3 marks)
steps: The matt black surface is a good absorber of infrared radiation.
The shiny silver surface reflects most of the radiation, so is a poor absorber.
More energy is absorbed by the black plate so its temperature rises more.

worked.ans: The 6000 K curve is higher at all wavelengths and its peak is at a shorter wavelength than the curve for the 4000 K star.
worked.q: A graph shows intensity against wavelength for a star at 6000 K and a star at 4000 K. Describe two differences between the curves. (3 marks)
steps: The hotter star has a higher intensity at every wavelength.
The peak of the hotter star is at a shorter wavelength.
The cooler star has a lower, broader peak at a longer wavelength.
